planting.note: Set container-grown shrubs in spring into humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in a site shielded from late frost and drying wind.

directions: This Chinese mountain species is prized among rhododendron collectors for flowers that can open violet-blue, lavender, or near-purple, a color range unusual among larger-leaved rhododendrons. It flowers in April on an upright, airy shrub with small aromatic leaves, and performs best where spring frost rarely lingers since open flowers and new growth are both frost-shy. Give it a sheltered woodland-edge spot with morning sun or filtered light and consistently moist, acidic soil. It pairs well underplanted with white- or pink-flowered rhododendrons to offset its blue tones.

planting.note: Plant in spring in deep, acidic, humus-rich soil with room to grow into a large multi-stemmed shrub; it tolerates more open sun than many species rhododendrons once established.

directions: One of the most garden-forgiving Chinese rhododendron species, this plant eventually becomes a large, rounded evergreen shrub with smooth glossy leaves and loose trusses of softly fragrant flowers ranging from pale lavender-pink to near white. Bloom comes in mid to late spring and is noted for carrying a true scent, a trait many showier hybrids lack. It accepts more sun than most woodland rhododendrons and has also been used as a breeding parent for cold-hardier fragrant hybrids. Site it where its eventual size will not crowd neighboring shade plants.

planting.note: Plant shallowly in spring or fall into acidic, well-drained soil with steady moisture, siting it in dappled woodland shade similar to its native Honshu mountain forest.

directions: Native to the mountains of northern Honshu rather than the island of Yakushima that gave the related R. yakushimanum its name, this species forms a dense, rounded shrub with leaves that carry a pale woolly indumentum beneath. Funnel-shaped flowers in shades of pink fading toward white open in early to mid spring over several weeks. It is a cold-tolerant, slow-growing species well suited to a shaded foundation bed or woodland border where a tidy evergreen habit is wanted year-round. Its genetic closeness to yakushimanum means it shares that species' reputation for dependable, compact garden performance.

planting.note: Plant in an ericaceous, compost-enriched bed in partial shade; its naturally compact habit suits smaller shaded borders without future crowding.

directions: This Japanese subalpine species is grown as much for its foliage as its flowers: new growth emerges in summer thickly coated in soft white to tan indumentum, giving the whole shrub a silvery sheen before the undersides mature to a woolly tan. Clear light pink, bell-shaped flowers that fade toward white open in May on a compact, slow-growing plant that rarely needs pruning to stay tidy. It is a good choice for a small shaded bed where a naturally dwarf rhododendron with strong winter structure is wanted. Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, evenly moist soil; flower buds set around late June, so avoid letting the root zone dry out through early summer.

directions: Collected from high-elevation forests of Taiwan, this species is highly variable in size, with alpine-origin plants staying quite dwarf while lower-elevation forms grow larger, so named selections differ noticeably in mature height. Rounded trusses of pink buds open to pale pink flowers flecked with deeper pink spots inside, typically in April or May. The thick, felted leaves hold interest even without bloom, making it as much a foliage plant as a flowering one, and it tolerates more shade than many species while still flowering best with some direct sun. Feed lightly with an ericaceous fertilizer in spring and again right after flowering.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, acidic soil with consistent moisture through late June when next season's flower buds are forming.

directions: Native to high ridgelines spanning southeast Tibet, Yunnan, and Sichuan, this species is valued for blue-green scaly foliage that sets it apart in a shade border even before it blooms. Loose clusters of funnel-shaped flowers in dusky pink, purple, or lilac-blue open in April and May against the glaucous leaves. It is an easygoing woodland species once established, adapting readily to typical garden conditions despite its remote high-elevation origin. Give it filtered light and protection from the harshest winter wind for the cleanest foliage color.

planting.note: Plant shallowly in acidic, woodsy, moist but well-drained soil; its mounded habit works well tucked into a shaded bed or rock garden edge.

directions: First collected in the alpine mountains of Sichuan, this is one of the most distinctive dwarf rhododendron species, forming a tidy, rounded dome of small, nearly circular leaves that emerge coppery-bronze before maturing to blue-green. Dainty, bell-shaped pink flowers hang from the branches in April and May, each noticeably large relative to the plant's small leaves. Its naturally compact, mounding shape makes it a long-term favorite for shaded rock gardens and smaller woodland borders where many rhododendron species would eventually outgrow the space. Plant it shallowly, since the shallow, fibrous roots are easily smothered by deep planting or heavy mulch.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, rich, well-drained soil in a partly shaded site; this species tolerates more cold and more sun than many species rhododendrons once established.

directions: Native to forests and open grasslands at high elevation in Sichuan and Yunnan, this species ranges from a low, dwarf shrublet in some forms to an upright plant several feet tall in others, so it pays to check a given selection's habit before siting it. Clouds of small, funnel-shaped pink flowers smother the red-stemmed branches in early to mid spring, often ahead of many other rhododendrons. The gray-green leaves release a spicy, almost rosemary-like scent when brushed or crushed, giving the plant a second season of interest beyond bloom. It is notably cold-hardy for a Chinese species rhododendron and takes more open sun than most of its relatives.
